brief.situation: 11:00 in an outpatient pelvic health clinic. You are the physical therapist. Ms. Rossi, 30, is 26 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated pregnancy and low back pain. She ran and did CrossFit before pregnancy and asks for 'a real workout plan'.
handover: Her obstetric provider has cleared her for exercise.
Clinic policy: stop exercise for warning signs and position a pregnant patient on her left side if she becomes symptomatic lying flat; tell her obstetric provider of any warning sign.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Why did she feel faint, and what plan do you give her?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: After the first trimester, lying flat lets the uterus compress the great vessels and drops blood pressure: supine hypotension.
parts.modelAnswer: Lying flat at 26 weeks, the baby's weight squeezes the big vessels and her pressure drops. That's why she got dizzy.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Turns her onto her left side, then prescribes about 150 minutes a week of moderate activity by the talk test, avoiding supine positions, contact and fall-risk sports and altitude changes, and teaches warning signs.
parts.modelAnswer: Roll her onto her left side, then give her about 150 minutes a week of moderate exercise by the talk test, no lying flat, no contact or fall-risk sports, and teach her when to stop.

scoring.modelReasoning: Exercise in pregnancy: about 150 minutes a week of moderate activity checked with the talk test, avoiding the supine position, contact sports, fall-risk sports and altitude changes, and stopping for warning signs. Ms. Rossi's dizziness flat on her back is supine hypotension: turn her onto her left side, then build her plan with inclined or side-lying positions.
